title: How to Love a Spouse Who Has Gone Cold
excerpt: When a marriage goes cold from one side, the temptation is to match the coldness. The harder and better road is to keep loving without a guarantee.
body:
There is a particular loneliness in lying next to someone who has gone cold. Not cruel, usually. Just absent. The warmth has drained out of them, the affection, the interest, and you do not know exactly when it happened or why, and your attempts to reach them keep landing on a surface that does not give. You are still married. You are not still close. And the worst part is that you cannot fix it alone, because it takes two to be close and only one to be distant.

I want to be honest with you about how hard this is before I say anything else, because cheap encouragement is an insult to people in this situation. This is one of the heaviest things a person can carry, and there is no technique that guarantees a thaw. What I can offer is a way to love and to stay whole while you do not yet know how it ends.

## First, try to find out why

Coldness is a symptom, not a cause, and the cause matters. A spouse goes cold for reasons, even if neither of you can name them yet. Accumulated resentment that never got cleared. A hurt you do not know you caused. Depression, which can drain warmth out of a person and has nothing to do with you, though it feels like it does. Exhaustion past the point of having anything to give. Sometimes something more serious, an affair of the heart or the body, a foot already partway out the door. The right response is different for each, so before you decide how to love them, try to understand what you are loving them through.

Ask, gently and without accusation. Not what is wrong with you, which is an attack, but I have felt a distance between us and I do not want to assume I know why, and I want to understand. Then be quiet long enough for an answer. You may not get one the first time. Ask again, another day, without making the asking itself a pressure.

## Do not match the coldness

The strongest pull, when someone goes cold, is to go cold back. To protect yourself by withdrawing first, to stop reaching so you stop getting hurt, to give them the distance they seem to want. It feels like dignity. It is mostly self-protection, and it accelerates exactly the thing you fear, because now both of you are withdrawing and the marriage cools twice as fast.

This is where the gospel asks something hard and specific. We love a God who kept loving while we were still cold to him, who did not wait for us to warm up before he moved toward us. Romans says that while we were still enemies, Christ died for us. The pattern of that love is movement toward distance, not away from it. To keep loving a cold spouse, in small and undramatic ways, without the guarantee of return, is one of the truest imitations of Christ a person can offer, and one of the most costly.

This does not mean groveling or chasing. It means refusing to let their coldness set your temperature. You keep the small warmth alive, the kind word, the made coffee, the touch on the shoulder, not as a transaction to earn warmth back, but because that is who you have decided to be regardless of what comes back. There is a strange freedom in this. When you love without requiring a return, the other person's coldness loses some of its power to control you.

## Stay whole while you wait

You cannot pour love from an empty self, and a person being slowly frozen out will run dry if they have no other source. So do not make your cold spouse the only well you drink from. This is where the rest of your life matters enormously, the friendships, the church, the work that has meaning, the God who promised never to leave or forsake even when a spouse has. A believer is anchored not in a spouse's responsiveness but in a Father who will never go cold, and that anchor is what keeps you from being destroyed by a marriage that is not, right now, giving you anything.

Do not isolate. The instinct in a cold marriage is to hide it, out of shame and loyalty, and the hiding leaves you alone with it. Find one or two safe people, a wise friend, a pastor, who can hold this with you and remind you who you are when the daily coldness starts to make you doubt it.

## Know the limits, and know the line

Keeping faith with a cold spouse is not the same as accepting harm. There is a difference, and it is the most important distinction in this whole piece. Coldness is one thing. Cruelty is another. If your spouse is not merely distant but controlling, frightening, or abusive, if there is violence, intimidation, or a fear in you about your safety, then this is no longer the situation I have been describing, and the counsel changes entirely. You do not owe an abuser the patient, hopeful love this article describes. You owe yourself and your children safety first. Get to a safe place and get help. In the United States you can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233, any hour. Forgiveness and faithfulness were never meant to be a chain that binds a person to harm.

For a marriage that is cold rather than dangerous, there is still a limit to what one person can carry alone, and reaching that limit is not a failure. If your reaching gets no response over a long season, it is right and wise to ask your spouse to go to counseling with you, and right to go yourself even if they will not. Loving a cold spouse does not mean accepting that nothing can change. It means refusing to give up on change while also refusing to let the waiting destroy you.

## This week

Do two things. First, find one moment to ask the gentle question, I have felt a distance, and I want to understand, not to accuse, and then listen without defending. Second, name one source of life outside the marriage that you have let go dry, a friendship, your time with God, something that is yours, and take one step back toward it this week, because you cannot keep loving from empty. And if what you are facing is not coldness but danger, do not wait. Get safe first. That is not the failure of love. It is the floor beneath it.
